title: Four kinds of happiness
hook: having wealth, using it well, owing no debt, and being blameless (AN 4.62)

segments.voice: Yesterday: five trades, and your line, what your money does. Did you follow one payment and see what it supports? Day three hundred seventy-nine.

Anathapindika was one of the richest men in the city of Savatthi. His name means feeder of the unprotected, because of how much food he gave away. By the old story, he bought a park for the Buddha's community by covering its ground in gold coins. So when the Buddha talks to him about money, he isn't lecturing someone on thrift. He's talking to a man who has more than enough. And he tells him there are four kinds of happiness that wealth can touch, and that one of them outweighs the other three put together. Today: four kinds of happiness.
screen: `FEEDER OF THE UNPROTECTED.` → `A PARK PAVED IN GOLD.` → `ONE OUTWEIGHS THE REST.`

segments.voice: The first is the happiness of having: knowing you have wealth earned, the sutta says, by hard work, by the strength of your arms and the sweat of your brow, rightly gained. Notice that this counts as a real happiness. The Buddha doesn't tell a householder that money is shameful. The second is the happiness of using it: enjoying your wealth and doing good with it, for yourself, your family, your friends, and worthy causes. Money sitting untouched is only half a pleasure. The third is the happiness of owing nothing, no debt, large or small. Anyone who has lain awake over a credit card bill knows exactly what this one feels like when it's missing. And the fourth is the happiness of blamelessness: knowing that what you've done with your body, your speech and your mind carries no fault. Then comes the verse at the end. The first three, the Buddha says, aren't worth a sixteenth part of the fourth. A sixteenth was the old Indian way of saying a tiny fraction. So the order is clear, but it isn't a choice between them. A householder can have all four. The sutta simply ranks them. You can be wealthy, generous and debt-free, and still lie awake if you know how the money was made. And you can have very little, owe nothing, and sleep like a stone, because there's nothing in your day you need to hide.
screen: `THE HAPPINESS OF HAVING.` · `THE HAPPINESS OF USING.` · `THE HAPPINESS OF OWING NOTHING.` · `BLAMELESSNESS OUTWEIGHS THEM ALL.` · then, large: `BLAMELESS IS BEST.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Go through the four slowly, one at a time, and look for any trace of each in your own life. Something you have, however small. Something you were able to use well, or share. A debt you've paid off, or never had. And something you did this week that you don't need to hide. Rest a little longer on whichever one you find. Let it be a real happiness, the way the sutta says it is. The bell holds the time.
Four kinds of happiness. Having, using, owing nothing, and blamelessness; the Buddha tells Anathapindika the last outweighs the rest.
Your line: blameless is best. Today, note one money blessing you have, and one thing you did that you'd be glad for anyone to see. Day three hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use this sutta to show that householders may rightly enjoy honestly earned wealth, while counting a clear conscience as the greatest happiness; Anathapindika is remembered in the tradition as the model generous lay follower.

fork.setup: you're Anathapindika, one of the richest men in Savatthi. of the four kinds of happiness, which does the Buddha say is worth the most?
fork.reveal: in AN 4.62 the Buddha says the first three aren't worth a sixteenth part of the happiness of blamelessness.

original.note: Pali anavajja-sukha: the happiness of blamelessness, the fourth and greatest in AN 4.62.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhism says money can't buy happiness.
what it means: rightly earned money brings three real happinesses, and blamelessness is worth far more than all three.
what a scholar hears: AN 4.62 names atthi-sukha, bhoga-sukha, anaṇa-sukha and anavajja-sukha, and its closing verse uses the old idiom of 'a sixteenth part' to rank them.

sources.ref: Vinaya, Cullavagga VI (Anathapindika buys Jeta's Grove)

notes: AN 4.62 paraphrased; the four Pali terms and the 'sixteenth part' verse given from memory. Confirm.
Anathapindika's name glossed as 'feeder of the unprotected' (anātha-piṇḍika, 'giver of alms to the helpless'); his personal name was Sudatta.
Jeta's Grove purchase with gold coins covering the ground: Vinaya Cullavagga VI; told as 'by the old story'.
'one of the richest men in Savatthi' softened from 'the richest'.
